interactions.summary: Jiang restates Dante's puzzle: if the soul naturally lunges toward beauty and can confuse beauty with possession, why would God build a moral system that seems to compel evil?
A student reads Virgil's answer that primal desire is morally neutral, while an inborn countermove sorts and restrains later longings; Beatrice will call that freedom free will.
Jiang translates Virgil's answer into an obedience model: free will is not following emotion but submitting desire to reason, authority, and mission, as Aeneas does against pity and passion.
The student begins a new passage in which Dante and Virgil encounter a shade rushing upward after the mountain has shaken.
Jiang situates the new scene: the earthquake marks a soul finishing purgation and hurrying toward heaven after clearing all seven terraces.

speaker_notes.note: SPEAKER_00 continues to function as the student reader of the assigned Dante passage, not as an independent discussant.
The quoted passage has ASR damage, but the recoverable core is clear: primal desire itself is morally neutral, while an inborn faculty curbs and judges later loves under the name of free will.

claims.claim: Jiang says Dante's free-will problem is that the soul naturally seeks what looks beautiful, so without another mechanism it is hard to explain how anyone can distinguish good from evil rather than merely follow compelled desire.
The Virgil passage read in class says primal inclinations and first desires are given in human beings like a bee's honey-making urge and therefore deserve neither praise nor blame in themselves.
The same passage argues that moral merit rests on an inborn power that counsels at the threshold of assent, gathering and winnowing good and evil longings.
Virgil's answer names free will as the power to curb love even when the source of love is necessary and not self-chosen.
Jiang interprets this Virgilian free will as obedience: reason is the capacity to restrain emotion by submitting to authority rather than trusting intuition.
Jiang says the Aeneid dramatizes this model by forcing Aeneas repeatedly to abandon rage, homeland attachment, erotic desire, and pity in order to obey his mission to found Rome.
For Jiang, Virgil's core claim is that love does not define the self; reason defined as obedience does, and demonstrating that obedience is what proves free will.
Jiang explains the next Purgatorio scene as an ascent checkpoint: when a soul finally clears all seven terraces, the mountain shakes like an earthquake to announce that the soul is about to ascend.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang makes the moral problem brutal: why would God create a system where the soul seems naturally compelled toward evil through beauty itself?
signature_moments.source_phrase: why would God create a system in which you are naturally compelled to do evil
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens the free-will problem into a direct indictment of the cosmos rather than a minor classroom puzzle.

signature_moments.moment: Free will appears as a threshold-keeper that winnows desire instead of generating desire from nothing.
signature_moments.source_phrase: keeper of the threshold of your assent
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's most compact image for Virgil's answer to moral responsibility.

signature_moments.moment: Reason gets stripped down to obedience, even when mercy feels more human than mission.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is Jiang's hardest compression of Virgil's anthropology and gives later Dante reversals something concrete to overturn.

glossary_terms.term: keeper of the threshold of assent
glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Virgil's image for the inborn faculty that judges whether desire should be indulged, restrained, or redirected.
In this Virgilian packet, free will is the power to curb desire through reason, which Jiang interprets as obedience to higher authority and mission.
The higher commanded purpose that must override emotion, pity, erotic attachment, and intuitive mercy in Jiang's reading of Aeneas.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-05-22 Jiang gives a dated strong-form Virgilian definition of free will as reasoned obedience rather than spontaneous self-expression; later packets on Dante's revolution should be read as replies to this exact framing.
